passage:
Teacher's note, Nursery B, Monday
Snack came late today because the kitchen was short of staff. Rajni asked, 'Is it time?' seven times and then cried on the mat, fists tight.
I didn't tell her to be a big girl. I turned over our blue sand timer and said, 'When the sand is all down, snack comes.' Gargi sat with her, and we sang the waiting-train song twice.
Rajni watched the sand the whole time, whispering, 'Almost, almost.' When it ran out, the snack trolley arrived. She clapped.
Plan: use the timer before every snack this week.

qa.q: How many times did Rajni ask 'Is it time?'
qa.a: Seven times.

qa.q: What do Rajni's tight fists suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest she felt frustrated and upset because waiting for the snack was very hard.

qa.q: What choice did the teacher make that helped Rajni wait?
qa.a: The teacher turned over the blue sand timer and sang the waiting-train song, making the wait something Rajni could see and do.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel sitting with Rajni during the song?
qa.a: Gargi may feel kind and useful, helping Rajni through a hard wait.

grounding: Shows a young child who cries when a treat is delayed, and a teacher who makes waiting concrete with a timer and a song.

passage:
On the rattling bus to Ajji's village, Chinmay asked, 'Are we there yet?' before the bus left the stand. Then at the first turn. Then at the petrol pump. By the sugar mill his face crumpled and he kicked the seat. 'I want Ajji NOW!'
His mother Manjula pulled him onto her lap. 'Let's play. Count the buffaloes. When you reach ten, we'll be at the big banyan tree, and after that it's Ajji's gate.'
'One!' Chinmay shouted. 'Two, a baby one!'
At nine his nose was on the window. At ten the banyan swept past. He jumped up. 'Now Ajji!'

qa.q: What did Manjula ask Chinmay to count?
qa.a: The buffaloes.

qa.q: How was Chinmay feeling when he kicked the seat by the sugar mill?
qa.a: He was frustrated and impatient; the long wait felt too hard, and he wanted Ajji right now.

qa.q: Which choice made the bus ride easier for Chinmay?
qa.a: Manjula turned the wait into a counting game with a clear marker, ten buffaloes to the banyan tree, so the time felt concrete.

qa.q: How might the other passengers feel once Chinmay starts counting buffaloes?
qa.a: They might feel relieved as the crying stops, and maybe amused by his shout of 'a baby one!'

grounding: Shows a young child who keeps asking if they are there yet, and a parent who makes the wait concrete with a small game.

passage: On the rattling bus to Nani's village, Bhupen asked, "Are we there yet?" for the ninth time. When his mother, Rajni, said the sweets from the bus stand would wait till Nani's house, he burst into tears and kicked the seat. Rajni didn't scold. "Let's count buffaloes. When we see ten, we'll be at the big banyan tree, and after that it's only one song till Nani's." Bhupen sniffed and pressed his face to the window. "One! Two!" At ten he shouted, and Rajni began the song. He sang along, wiping his nose.

qa.q: How many times had Bhupen asked "Are we there yet?"
qa.a: Nine times.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen burst into tears?
qa.a: He was frustrated and upset that the sweets had to wait, and waiting felt too hard.

qa.q: How did Rajni make the waiting easier?
qa.a: She turned it into a counting game and a song, so Bhupen could see the wait getting shorter.

qa.q: What is it like for Rajni to hear the same question nine times?
qa.a: Rajni is probably tired, but she stays patient and finds a game instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a young child who cries over a delayed treat and repeats "are we there yet", helped by a parent's counting game and song.

passage: Dalia's fifth-birthday cake wouldn't be ready until eleven, and at breakfast in their Cairo flat she was already wailing. "I want it NOW!" Her mother, Selin, set the big kitchen timer on the counter. "When this rings, we go to the bakery. Let's see what we can do before it rings." They built a tower of cups. They sang the birthday song twice. Dalia checked the timer every few minutes, bouncing on her toes. When it finally rang, she shrieked and ran for her shoes.

qa.q: When would the cake be ready?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: How was Dalia feeling at breakfast?
qa.a: She was impatient and upset, wailing that she wanted the cake now.

qa.q: Why did the timer help Dalia?
qa.a: It made the wait concrete, so she could see when it would end, and filled the time with games.

qa.q: How might Selin feel when Dalia runs for her shoes?
qa.a: Selin likely feels relieved and pleased that the wait ended happily.

grounding: Illustrates a young child who finds waiting for a treat very hard, helped by a timer and small games.

passage: At the kindergarten in Pune, snack time was at eleven, and by ten Sonali was already at the door. "Is it snack time? Is it now? Now?" When Rehana-ma'am said "Not yet," she flopped onto the mat and cried. Rehana-ma'am brought out the big sand timer. "When the sand runs out, it's snack time. Can you help me watch it?" She added a finger game, "five little mangoes", to sing while the sand fell. Sonali watched, sniffing, then singing. When the last grains slipped through, she jumped up. "It's done! Snack!"

qa.q: What time was snack time?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel when told "Not yet"?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and sad, flopping onto the mat and crying.

qa.q: What did Rehana-ma'am do that helped?
qa.a: She used a sand timer and a finger song to make the wait visible and fun.

qa.q: How might the other children see Sonali watching the timer?
qa.a: They might want to join in and watch the sand too, making the wait a shared game.

grounding: Shows a young child for whom waiting is very hard, helped by a teacher's sand timer and song.

passage:
Monday. Pankaj pressed his nose to the car window. "Are we there yet? Are we there yet?" When Mama said the ice cream shop was after the bridge, he kicked the seat and cried.
Wednesday. Before leaving for Nani's, Mama gave him a paper strip with five stickers. "Each time we pass a petrol pump, peel one off." Pankaj counted pumps and asked only twice.
Saturday. Damini, his cousin, whined in the queue for the merry-go-round. Pankaj took her hand. "Let's sing the elephant song. When it ends, we'll be closer." They sang it three times, and then it was their turn.

qa.q: What did Mama give Pankaj on Wednesday?
qa.a: She gave him a paper strip with five stickers to peel off at each petrol pump.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj kick the seat and cry on Monday?
qa.a: He was frustrated and impatient; the ice cream shop still felt far away and he could not bear the wait.

qa.q: What could a parent borrow from Mama's idea for a long wait?
qa.a: They could make the wait something a child can see and count, like stickers, a song or a small game.

qa.q: How might Damini feel when Pankaj starts singing with her in the queue?
qa.a: She probably feels comforted and less bored, because the song gives the wait a clear end she can hear.

grounding: Pankaj's crying over a delayed treat eases as adults make waiting concrete with stickers and songs, which he later shares with his cousin.
